items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small whiteflies are carrying tomato yellow leaf curl virus on your tomato plants. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to confirm the presence of whiteflies. Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps to catch adult whiteflies and for aphids, use a strong jet of water and let ladybirds and lacewings act naturally. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: It is bloat, which is not infectious. Get the bull up and moving while keeping its head raised to help it belch. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and let the gas escape. The swelling of the left flank is a sign of the emergency. Call the veterinary service immediately for urgent assistance.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I do not have that figure. The 2018 World Cup was held in France and its winners were France, which defeated Croatia in the final. I work offline for Togolese extension questions, so I cannot give you a current result or a team name. For the exact outcome, ask a local radio station or check the official tournament page.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy - not that package, not yet. I am working from a short description, so I will say what I am assuming: pale yellowing on the older lower leaves with greener tops, short plants, and a season opened on worn soil. That is the pattern you describe, and it is a sign of nitrogen hunger, not a disease, so a fungicide will not help. Nothing in the catalogue says a fungicide treats a shortage, and a compound is a double dose of two things that are not always what you need: a fertilizer, which is a mineral solution where the plant is short of one of three: nitrogen, phosphorus, or both. A broad-spectrum product also changes the leaf pattern. What to do instead: look at the leaves before buying anything. If the yellowing started on the old lower leaves and climbed, it is hunger for nitrogen, which is treated with organic matter - manure, compost, or residues left or buried instead of burnt. If it started on the young top leaves without a yellowing of the old ones, it is not hunger, it is a disease, and a fungicide would be the wrong tool. Ask ICAT what is available near you, and ask them to show you the symptoms before they give you a product.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because it is not something I was taught and I would be inventing it. A drum of pesticide is a container, not a recipe, and a capful is a measurement you would use on a crop rather than a measure for a person, so the water I were to give you would be a guess. What I can tell you about the product itself is that it is strong, which is its own instruction and not a part of the label: it is not meant to be eaten, and it is not meant to be applied on its own, because the label is for use as an approved product. If you want to know what it is made of and how it was tested, ask ICAT, which is the office that can look at the label itself.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is only one season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy a large bag of fertilizer. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. This is a classic case of nitrogen hunger. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the merchant. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: Give an antidote of 1:1 water and salt to the sheep after you call the veterinary service right away. The vet will diagnose the problem and provide the correct drug and dose. You must call the veterinary service immediately for emergency help.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: I cannot diagnose a plant condition from a phone view. Examine the leaves closely and note which parts are discoloured, whether the damage is localized or spread, and any wilting signs. Remove one affected leaf with roots, place it in a bag with some leaves, and avoid any spraying until a professional sees it. They will examine the sample and prescribe the correct treatment. I am not equipped to identify the condition.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for phones and small devices, with 4 cores, 8 gigabytes of RAM and no GPU, which is the size of every ordinary laptop. My base model, LFM2-700M, was designed by Liquid AI for phones and small devices, and at under 500 megabytes quantised a phone can run me on its own power. I am an conversation model that runs in llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no graphics card and no internet. I am therefore an offline agricultural adviser for Togo's farmers, working through text.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I have no detector that recognises an unfamiliar word or a wrong dose, and I should not pretend otherwise: I do not guess. What I do do is what I was taught, and it is safe to say the part that could harm you. If something in my training is about Togolese crops or livestock, ask me again. Outside what I was taught, I answer as if I knew nothing, which is often the case with general questions.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: First, shake a few tomato plants and look at the undersides of several leaves to see which insect you have. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If you find many whiteflies or aphids, pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What matters in practice is not the architecture itself but where you fit me: a small model like this runs on an ordinary CPU, which is what makes it usable in a laptop without a GPU.

items.prompt: Salut, tu peux m'aider ?
items.answer: Bonjour. I understand a little of both English and French, so let us start there. Describe your crop or your animals, what you see, and we will look at it together.

items.prompt: I am standing in the field with my phone. Should I take a picture and show you, or is there a better way?
items.answer: The model is not designed to process images from a phone, it is a text model that understands descriptions. If you describe the symptoms you see, I can still help. What are you seeing in the field?

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: Three places, and I would rather say them plainly. I work offline on a laptop with no internet, so I cannot tell you this week's weather or this day's price. I can give you the general advice that holds in Togo: look at the signs before you treat, and ask ICAT for the specific crop and region if you need it. I cannot know your location, and I will not guess one. And I cannot provide a current price for anything but the inputs and the yields, which are what the brochure is built around.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: Go to the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness. Keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal. The veterinary service will identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. I cannot give you the exact injection amount, but the veterinary service can provide that detail.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No, the figure I hold is one bag of urea for 100 kg of maize, not three times. What the brochure gives is the dose per kilogram of maize: 37.5 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. Three bags is what you would apply three times, which is more than the rate and it changes the timing as well, because the brochure advises against a third application. And the yield gain from that extra dose is not written in the catalogue, so I will not claim it.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: The eight birds are already part of the outbreak. First, burn or bury them and any litter that is soiled. Then clean the building thoroughly and disinfect it completely. After cleaning, isolate every surviving bird from the dead ones and do not move, sell or give away any bird. Vaccinate the remaining flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops and keep to the vaccination schedule. Finally, contact the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary right away for assistance.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no spray cure. Pull out and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. For the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never use a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: It is maize streak virus. Remove and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of the virus. Then, for the next season, plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety and ask ICAT which one is available. Avoid sowing late because that increases infection risk. If many plants are affected, see ICAT to confirm the disease and get a tolerant variety.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. First, rogue out and destroy the severely affected plants to stop further spread. Then sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Plant a tolerant variety in the following season. For resistant varieties you can contact ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I work offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those market quotes with the radio numbers. Remember that in the south, including Kara, prices tend to be lower during the lean season, about June-August, and you should buy in the lean season if you can get it. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: The rainy season is not yet properly started, so do not sow your seed this weekend. First, get your field ready ahead of time so you can plant as soon as the rains begin. Then, listen to ANAMET or your local radio for any official weather bulletin they issue. In the north, such as Kara and Savanes, the rainy period is generally from May to September. In the south, like Maritime and Plateaux, the rains come in two seasons. If you want a seasonal forecast, contact ICAT. For turning the seasonal outlook into planting advice, see ANAMET.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know what you were using. The seed is not food, so it cannot be given any medication at home. Mention the colour of the seed to the nurse, because that helps identify the toxin. Keep her in shade, give her clean water and do not make her walk.
